Organisation.intro: Multicellular organisms are organised into a hierarchy of increasing complexity. Understanding this hierarchy is essential for B2.

sections.title: The Hierarchy of Organisation
numbered: Tissues — groups of similar cells working together (e.g. muscle tissue)
Organs — groups of different tissues working together (e.g. stomach)
Organ systems — groups of organs working together (e.g. digestive system)

callout.label: Memory Aid
callout.text: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ System → Organism. Remember: 'C-T-O-O-O' or 'Cells Typically Organise Organisms Outstandingly'.

keyTerms.def: A group of similar cells working together to carry out a specific function
A structure made of different tissues working together to perform a function
A group of organs working together to perform a major function

examTips: Know the correct order of the hierarchy — cells are the smallest, organisms the largest.
Be able to give examples at each level: e.g. muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart → cardiovascular system.
commonMistakes: Reversing the order of the hierarchy.
Confusing a tissue (same cells) with an organ (different tissues).

Digestion.intro: Digestion is the process of breaking down large food molecules into smaller ones that can be absorbed into the bloodstream. Enzymes are key to this process.

sections.title: Enzymes in Digestion
points: Amylase — breaks down starch into sugars; produced in salivary glands and pancreas; works in mouth and small intestine
Protease — breaks down proteins into amino acids; produced in stomach, pancreas, small intestine
Lipase — breaks down fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol; produced in pancreas and small intestine

sections.title: The Digestive System
points: Mouth — mechanical digestion; amylase in saliva begins starch digestion
Oesophagus — moves food to stomach by peristalsis
Stomach — produces HCl (pH 2) to kill bacteria and activate pepsin; protease digestion
Small intestine — main site of digestion and absorption; villi increase surface area
Large intestine — absorbs water; compacts waste into faeces
Liver — produces bile; Pancreas — produces enzymes and sends to small intestine

sections.title: Bile
sections.text: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the small intestine.
points: Emulsifies fats — breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones
This increases the surface area for lipase to work on
Bile is alkaline — neutralises stomach acid in the small intestine
Bile is NOT an enzyme — it does not break down fats chemically

keyTerms.def: A biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions without being used up
Enzyme that breaks down starch into simple sugars
Enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids
Enzyme that breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Alkaline liquid produced by the liver that emulsifies fats
Breaking large fat droplets into smaller droplets to increase surface area

examTips: Bile is NOT an enzyme — it physically breaks up fat droplets (emulsification) rather than chemically digesting them.
Know where each enzyme is produced AND where it acts — these are often different places.
The stomach is acidic (HCl); the small intestine is alkaline (bile neutralises the acid).
commonMistakes: Saying bile digests fats — bile only emulsifies (physically breaks up) fats.
Forgetting that amylase works in the mouth as well as the small intestine.
Confusing where enzymes are MADE with where they WORK.

Heart and Circulation.intro: The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood around the body through a double circulatory system. Understanding its structure and function is key to B2.

sections.title: Double Circulatory System
points: Pulmonary circulation — heart → lungs → heart (picks up oxygen, drops off CO₂)
Systemic circulation — heart → body → heart (delivers oxygen, picks up CO₂)
The heart acts as a double pump — right side pumps to lungs; left side pumps to body

sections.title: Structure of the Heart
points: 4 chambers: left and right atria (upper), left and right ventricles (lower)
Valves — prevent backflow of blood (atrioventricular valves and semilunar valves)
Left ventricle has thicker walls — pumps blood to the whole body (higher pressure needed)
Right ventricle has thinner walls — pumps blood to the nearby lungs only
Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen

sections.title: Blood Vessels
points: Arteries — carry blood AWAY from the heart; thick muscular walls; high pressure
Veins — carry blood TO the heart; thin walls; low pressure; have valves to prevent backflow
Capillaries — very narrow; walls one cell thick; site of exchange between blood and tissues

keyTerms.def: Upper chamber of the heart that receives blood
Lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out
Flap in the heart or vein that prevents backflow of blood
Blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure
Blood vessel that carries blood towards the heart at low pressure
Tiny blood vessel with walls one cell thick where exchange occurs

examTips: Left ventricle has thicker walls than right — it pumps blood the full length of the body.
Arteries ALWAYS carry blood away from the heart (even pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs).
Veins have valves; arteries do not (they rely on high pressure).
commonMistakes: Saying arteries always carry oxygenated blood — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.
Confusing atria and ventricles — atria receive blood, ventricles pump it out.
Forgetting why the left ventricle has thicker walls.

Blood.intro: Blood is a tissue made up of several components, each with a specific function. Understanding these components is essential for B2.

sections.title: Components of Blood
points: Red blood cells — contain haemoglobin; carry oxygen; biconcave disc shape; no nucleus (more room for haemoglobin)
White blood cells — part of the immune system; fight infection; phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies
Platelets — small cell fragments; trigger blood clotting at wounds
Plasma — yellow liquid; transports: digested food, CO₂, urea, hormones, heat

sections.title: Red Blood Cells
sections.text: Red blood cells are highly adapted for carrying oxygen:
points: Biconcave disc shape — increases surface area for oxygen absorption
No nucleus — more space for haemoglobin
Flexible — can squeeze through narrow capillaries
Haemoglobin + O₂ → oxyhaemoglobin (in lungs)
Oxyhaemoglobin → haemoglobin + O₂ (at body tissues)

keyTerms.def: Red protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen
White blood cell that engulfs and destroys pathogens
White blood cell that produces antibodies
Liquid component of blood that transports dissolved substances
Cell fragments that help blood clot at wounds

examTips: Red blood cells have no nucleus — this is an adaptation allowing more haemoglobin and therefore more oxygen carried.
Plasma transports many things — CO₂, urea, hormones, glucose, amino acids, heat.
Know the two types of white blood cells: phagocytes (engulf) and lymphocytes (antibodies).
commonMistakes: Saying red blood cells carry carbon dioxide — they mainly carry oxygen (CO₂ is mostly carried in plasma).
Forgetting that platelets are cell fragments, not whole cells.

Heart Disease.intro: Coronary heart disease is one of the most common diseases in the UK. Understanding its causes, symptoms, and treatments is important for B2.

sections.title: Coronary Heart Disease (CHD)
sections.text: CHD occurs when fatty deposits (plaques) build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.
points: Fatty deposits = atherosclerosis
Reduced blood flow → less oxygen to heart muscle
Can cause angina (chest pain) or heart attack
Risk factors: smoking, high fat diet, lack of exercise, obesity, high blood pressure, genetics

sections.title: Treatments
points: Statins — drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels, slowing plaque build-up
Stents — metal mesh tubes inserted into arteries to keep them open
Bypass surgery — a healthy blood vessel is used to reroute blood around the blocked artery
Artificial heart valves — replace damaged valves; can be mechanical or biological

sections.title: Lifestyle Changes
points: Stop smoking — nicotine raises blood pressure; CO reduces oxygen in blood
Reduce saturated fat intake — lowers LDL cholesterol
Regular exercise — strengthens heart muscle, reduces blood pressure
Maintain healthy weight — reduces strain on heart

keyTerms.def: Blood vessels that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood
Build-up of fatty deposits (plaques) in artery walls, narrowing the lumen
Drug used to lower blood cholesterol levels
A mesh tube inserted into a narrowed artery to keep it open
Chest pain caused by restricted blood flow to the heart muscle

examTips: Statins reduce cholesterol — they slow plaque build-up but don't remove existing plaques.
Stents keep arteries open mechanically; bypass surgery creates a new route for blood flow.
Be able to evaluate treatments — consider risks vs benefits.
commonMistakes: Saying statins dissolve plaques — they only prevent new ones forming by reducing cholesterol.
Confusing coronary arteries (supply the heart) with pulmonary arteries (go to lungs).

Cancer.intro: Cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division. Understanding the difference between benign and malignant tumours, and the risk factors for cancer, is required for B2.

sections.title: What is Cancer?
sections.text: Cancer occurs when mutations in the genes that control cell division cause cells to divide uncontrollably, forming a mass called a tumour.
points: Mutations can be caused by: carcinogens (e.g. chemicals in cigarettes), radiation (UV, X-rays), some viruses
Some cancers are linked to inherited genetic mutations

sections.title: Benign vs Malignant Tumours
points: Benign tumour — stays in one place, does not invade other tissues, not cancerous, usually not life-threatening
Malignant tumour — cancerous; cells break away and spread via blood/lymph to other organs (metastasis); life-threatening

callout.label: Key Distinction
callout.text: Benign = stays put. Malignant = spreads (metastasises). Only malignant tumours are truly cancer.

keyTerms.def: A mass of abnormal cells formed by uncontrolled cell division
A tumour that remains in one location and does not spread
A cancerous tumour whose cells spread to other parts of the body
The spread of cancer cells from the primary tumour to other parts of the body
A substance that causes cancer by mutating DNA

examTips: Always distinguish between benign (non-spreading) and malignant (spreading/cancer) tumours.
Cancer = uncontrolled mitosis due to DNA mutations.
commonMistakes: Saying all tumours are cancer — only malignant tumours are cancerous.
Forgetting that cancer is caused by mutations in cell division genes, not just any mutation.

Plant Organisation.intro: Plants are also organised into tissues and organs. The leaf is the main organ for photosynthesis and understanding its structure is important for B2.

sections.title: Plant Tissues
points: Epidermal tissue — covers the outer surface of leaves and stems; waxy cuticle reduces water loss
Palisade mesophyll — packed with chloroplasts; main site of photosynthesis
Spongy mesophyll — air spaces for gas exchange; some photosynthesis
Xylem — transports water and mineral ions up from roots; dead cells forming hollow tubes
Phloem — transports dissolved sugars (sucrose) from leaves to rest of plant

sections.title: The Leaf
sections.text: The leaf is the main photosynthetic organ, adapted to maximise light absorption and gas exchange:
points: Broad flat surface — maximises light absorption
Thin — short diffusion distance for gases
Many stomata (mainly lower surface) — allow CO₂ in and O₂ out
Stomata controlled by guard cells — open in light, close in dark

sections.title: Transpiration
sections.text: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves through stomata. It drives water up through xylem.
points: Factors that increase transpiration: higher temperature, lower humidity, wind, more light
Measured using a potometer (measures water uptake as a proxy for transpiration)

keyTerms.def: Plant tissue that transports water and mineral ions upwards from roots
Plant tissue that transports sugars from leaves to the rest of the plant
The loss of water vapour from leaves through the stomata
Tiny pores in leaves that allow gas exchange and water vapour to escape
Cells that surround stomata and control their opening and closing

examTips: Xylem transports water UP; phloem transports sugars (translocation) both up and down.
Transpiration is affected by temperature, humidity, wind speed and light intensity.
Stomata open in light (photosynthesis needs CO₂) and close in dark or when water is scarce.
commonMistakes: Saying phloem transports water — it transports sugars. Xylem transports water.
Forgetting that xylem cells are dead (their walls form hollow tubes).
Confusing transpiration (water loss) with translocation (sugar transport in phloem).
